messages.author: 3a775dfa0a96bf95
messages.subject: ggplot feedback
parts:
Hadley,

ggplot2 is fantastic.  I have gotten amazing things done with it of immediate value to my work, and seen things in my data that I probably wouldn't have simply because it would have been too much trouble to set up the necessary graphs in other systems.

The ggplot2 book is also fantastic -- congratulations again on getting it to the publisher.

I do have some feedback for you on things that could increase ggplot's takeup by new users.  It is easy to focus on cool new features (including ones that I ask for...), more beautiful output, and so on, but there are other matters that are also important to users: error handling, display consistency, and documentation.

First of all, it seems to me that ggplot generally does a poor job of detecting bad input and giving error messages that make sense to users.  If I omit an aes where it wants one, or nest things incorrectly, or misspell something, or have an empty data frame, etc. etc., I usually get internal error messages ("attempt to apply non-function" is a popular one) from routines that ggplot is calling, usually without mentioning what part of the input is incorrect.  Traceback doesn't help; it just shows more *internal* detail.  Even when the error message is meaningful ("undefined columns selected"), it (a) doesn't give the name of the column in question or its context (was it in a facet spec? a group spec? an aes?), and (b) the error comes from an internal call to `[.data.frame` rather than from some part of ggplot.  I realize that handling errors cleanly can often take as much code as handling the correct cases correctly, but that (alas) is the nature of quality software.  I also realize that much other R software shares the same flaw, but it is still a flaw.

Secondly, on-screen display should be identical to output in other output forms (notably pdf).  It is frustrating to create a perfect plot on-screen only to discover that it is illegible on paper (especially since paper has higher resolution...) because legends overlap etc.

Third, the documentation needs to be filled out -- I believe this is already planned.  In the meantime, perhaps the man pages, instead of reading "All documentation is available at <URL: http://had.co.nz/ggplot2>." could point to the specific URL on had.co.nz.  Also, it would be useful to have some documentation on how the user can write new geom's, new stat's, etc.

Thanks again for a fantastic package.

           -s

publishing novel research.

If you could provide a large set of such problems then I could spend a
couple of hours and make many improvements to error reporting, rather
than attacking them piece-by-piece as I do now.

> Secondly, on-screen display should be identical to output in other output
> forms (notably pdf).  It is frustrating to create a perfect plot on-screen
> only to discover that it is illegible on paper (especially since paper has
> higher resolution...) because legends overlap etc.

Some of this is out of my control - rendering a plot on disk should
produce identical output to on-screen, so when it doesn't happen it
usually reflects a bug in base R. Such bugs really need to be
reported up stream, so minimal reproducible examples really help, as
well as the time and energy (and thick skin) required to shepherd the
bug through r-devel to actually get a fix.

> Third, the documentation needs to be filled out -- I believe this is already
> planned.  In the meantime, perhaps the man pages, instead of reading "All
> documentation is available at <URL: http://had.co.nz/ggplot2>." could point

There shouldn't be any of these left - but it's quite possible there
are :( ggplot2 documentation should be the most accessible area for
actually contributing patches.

> to the specific URL on had.co.nz.  Also, it would be useful to have some
> documentation on how the user can write new geom's, new stat's, etc.

I've made some efforts on this in the past, but it's a lot of work,
because I need to describe more of the internals of ggplot, which
still aren't completely fixed. (Especially when I start writing about
them and realise a better way to do it).

Hadley

On Fri, May 8, 2009 at 2:03 PM, hadley wickham <h.wi...@gmail.com> wrote:
>> there are other matters that are also important to users: error handling, display

Perhaps this would make a good M.S. thesis topic (or even an ambitious
undergraduate Independent Study) in your Computer Science
department...? e.g. "Incorporating user-friendly, modular error
handling in an advanced plotting package". Could be an interesting
software engineering topic, though R is of course not a mainstream
programming language and might be hard to sell to your CS colleagues
and students.
> If you could provide a large set of such problems then I could spend a couple of hours and make many improvements to error reporting, rather than attacking them piece-by-piece as I do now.
I'll try to do that.

>> Secondly, on-screen display should be identical to output in other output forms (notably pdf).  It is frustrating to create a perfect plot on-screen only to discover that it is illegible on paper (especially since paper has higher resolution...) because legends overlap etc.

Well, one approach would be to have the online display use something
like Display Postscript (whatever the current version of that is);
isn't that essentially what is done by the Draw package on the Mac?
That might slow down rendering, but at least ensures consistency
between screen display and paper. Maybe there's even a way to
configure Draw to do that today?

-s
